narrative:
The model determined that you have a 92% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in your third year of law school had the greatest influence, followed by your LSAT score, then your first-year performance. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year grades placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked near the middle. This low standing signaled to the model a pattern of academic difficulty that is hard to overcome on the bar exam. Your LSAT score of 26 was also well below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, further increasing the predicted risk of failure. Finally, your first-year grades similarly placed you at the very bottom of your class, reinforcing the same concern.

Although your upper-middle family income, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the decision, the academic signals were simply too consistent and too far from the successful group for the model to predict a passing outcome.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, seeking targeted academic support in your remaining law school courses, and exploring bar exam preparation programs designed for students with similar profiles. These steps could meaningfully change your prospects for future applications or for passing the bar itself. (248 words)
